hypotheses.claim: H1. Task complexity, not model size, predicts fit for Enterprise tasks
hypotheses.measurement: Per-pillar score against parameter count and cost per task, with a complexity rating per task
hypotheses.confirmedIf: Most pillars plateau at a mid-size or small model class; score correlates with task complexity more than with model size
hypotheses.refutedIf: Scores keep rising with model size across most pillars, including bounded tasks

hypotheses.claim: H2. Frontier upgrades do not move Enterprise-relevant metrics
hypotheses.measurement: Re-run the full task library on each new frontier release and compare with the incumbent on the pillars we use
hypotheses.confirmedIf: Public benchmark gains are large while TL Index pillar movement is within noise, except on named reasoning-heavy pillars
hypotheses.refutedIf: Each release moves several TL Index pillars past the production bar where the incumbent fell short

hypotheses.claim: H3. Task-specific trained smaller models beat general models in Enterprise context
hypotheses.measurement: For each pillar, a fine-tuned or distilled specialist against the best general model at equal latency budget, with retraining cost included
hypotheses.confirmedIf: Specialists win on bounded pillars (1, 3-routing, 7, 14, 15) at lower cost, and the gap holds across two quarterly re-runs
hypotheses.refutedIf: General models match specialists at similar cost, or specialist gains erode between re-runs faster than retraining is affordable

hypotheses.claim: H1 (company version). Admitted agent purposes cluster to the Domain candidates plus a platform set, with several purposes per domain sharing a model recipe
hypotheses.measurement: Admission ledger (owner, volume, data) plus task-mining clusters over the flagship and gateway logs
hypotheses.confirmedIf: By the end of wave 1, servicing (Advice), Compliance and Judge each hold three or more admitted purposes with named owners
hypotheses.refutedIf: A domain holds one or fewer admitted purposes after a quarter; TL-011 should not carry it as a Domain model

hypotheses.claim: H2 (lab, near-circular). Most multi-model agents are Core plus a judge, so the Judge family is the shared dependency and the first platform build
hypotheses.measurement: Model recipe per admitted purpose; demand counts in the capability catalogue
hypotheses.confirmedIf: 70% or more of admitted multi-model purposes carry a judge component and the Judge family holds the highest demand count
hypotheses.refutedIf: Fewer than half carry one, or deterministic checks replace the judge in most

hypotheses.claim: H3 (lab, proxy). Methodology variants of one purpose differ enough that the choice matters, and the simplest variant does not always win
hypotheses.measurement: Each wave-1 purpose in two variants x two levels on declared public or synthetic data, paired tests, 3+ seeds: house rubric, cost per task, latency, pass^k
hypotheses.confirmedIf: For at least two purposes, variants differ by more than 5 rubric points, or by 2x on cost at equal quality
hypotheses.refutedIf: Variants within 3 points and 1.5x cost on all purposes: stop building variants, ship the simplest build (kill criterion I-5)

hypotheses.claim: H4 (lab, provisional). The winning variant on TLM4 Core with the house judge matches a frontier baseline at lower cost, with data inside the boundary
hypotheses.measurement: Same inputs and frontier-panel judge for both arms, plus a human-graded audit by Jithin (one grader, disclosed)
hypotheses.confirmedIf: Within 3 points of the frontier at half the cost or less
hypotheses.refutedIf: The frontier leads by more than 3 points after one retrain cycle; that purpose is not evidence for a Domain model

hypotheses.claim: H5 (company version). A compared, adoptable variant is picked up by a business team without ThinkLatent engineering
hypotheses.measurement: Teams using a library variant within 60 days of publication; time from request to first use
hypotheses.confirmedIf: Two or more teams adopt a wave-1 purpose within 60 days; first use inside two weeks
hypotheses.refutedIf: No adoption outside the originating team

hypotheses.claim: H6 (company version). Wave 1 reduces human time on its two business purposes without losing recall
hypotheses.measurement: After-call minutes per call; pre-review reviewer minutes per item and recall on known true positives, frozen pre/post window
hypotheses.confirmedIf: 30% less after-call time; 40% less reviewer time at no loss of recall
hypotheses.refutedIf: No change, or recall drops; the agent is withdrawn from that queue

hypotheses.claim: H7 (lab, narrowed). A change of harness or serving configuration moves pass^k materially on one Core version; the Core-version comparison waits for the company version
hypotheses.measurement: Each wave-1 purpose across two serving configurations on one pinned Core version, pass^k on the index
hypotheses.confirmedIf: The serving-configuration delta exceeds 5 pass^k points on at least two purposes
hypotheses.refutedIf: Serving-configuration deltas sit within noise; harness variants are not worth a stream

hypotheses.claim: H8 (company version). Shown quality, cost, latency and reliability side by side, business teams choose variants on the measured frontier
hypotheses.measurement: The index logs each team's choice beside the comparison card
hypotheses.confirmedIf: 70% or more of choices sit on the accuracy-cost frontier
hypotheses.refutedIf: Choices cluster on a dominated variant; the comparison card is redesigned

killCriteria.criterion: I-1. A declared dataset for each purpose (public or synthetic, provenance written), with what it can and cannot prove
killCriteria.action: Fewer than 2 of 3 purposes have one: park the purposes without one

killCriteria.criterion: I-2. TL-004 (TL Index) week-4 gate met, with S-E's first task set delivered
killCriteria.checked: Read as a start condition at week 8
killCriteria.action: Gate missed, or the task set missing because of TL-012: release S-E and cut wave 1 to one purpose (pre-review)

killCriteria.criterion: I-3. Judge stand-in agreement with a human-graded audit of 100 or more items per purpose
killCriteria.action: Agreement below 0.6: H3 and H4 become descriptive only and drive no publish decision

killCriteria.criterion: I-4. Weekly review slots for TL-012 kept by Jithin (Tuesday, Friday)
killCriteria.action: 2 slots missed in a row: TL-012 leaves Building (D-152)

killCriteria.criterion: I-5. H3: paired variant deltas with 95% intervals
killCriteria.action: All purposes within 3 points and 1.5x cost, or intervals wider than +/-5 points: stop building variants and ship variant A only

killCriteria.criterion: I-6. Engineer-weeks and review hours burned against plan
killCriteria.action: More than 60% of either burned with no purpose past its first comparison: park at the circuit breaker, never extend

killCriteria.criterion: Pre-review: recall and precision on a frozen labelled set of 200 or more known violations
killCriteria.checked: Set by end of week 8, read week 11
killCriteria.action: No set in time: park. Recall below 0.95 or precision below 0.5: withdraw

killCriteria.criterion: Task mining: cluster stability across two seeds; clusters above the privacy threshold (set at the spike start) that map to a named Domain candidate
killCriteria.action: Stability below 0.7 adjusted Rand, or fewer than 3 mappable clusters: kill the spike and read H1 from the admission ledger

killCriteria.criterion: After-call: (a) proposals touching protected fields on an injection test set; (b) variant A field accuracy against the frontier baseline; (c) TL-008 shaped
killCriteria.action: (a) any such proposal: stop the purpose. (b) more than 5 points behind after the optimised level: park. (c) not shaped: variant A only

hypotheses.claim: H1. A DFlash or EAGLE-3 drafter trained on the served model reaches a mean accepted length of at least 3.5 on service-level calls at temperature 0.3 or lower
hypotheses.measurement: Mean accepted tokens per verify step on held-out service-level prompts
hypotheses.confirmedIf: 3.5 or more
hypotheses.refutedIf: Under 2.5: the 27B cannot pass 1,000 tok/s on H100; the 200 ms class moves to the 7B Core, shorter replies or faster silicon

hypotheses.claim: H2. One 8x H100 node serving the Core 27B at TP8 with that drafter gives at least 1,000 tok/s per request at p50 with up to 8 in flight
hypotheses.measurement: tok/s per request at 1, 4 and 8 in flight in the proof grid
hypotheses.confirmedIf: p50 of 1,000 tok/s or more at 8 in flight
hypotheses.refutedIf: p50 under 1,000 at 8 in flight

hypotheses.claim: H3. 4-bit weights (W4A16 on H100, NVFP4 on Blackwell) stay within 1 point of FP8 on the TL Index tasks of the fast-lane use cases
hypotheses.measurement: TL Index task scores, 4-bit against FP8
hypotheses.confirmedIf: Within 1 point overall and no task worse by more than 2
hypotheses.refutedIf: Any task drops more than 2 points: stay on FP8

hypotheses.claim: H4. The 7B Core with its drafter returns 300-token replies in 200 ms or less at p95 with up to 8 in flight per TP4 replica across 1,000 to 10,000-token prompts, and the TL Index shows it sufficient on those use cases
hypotheses.measurement: End-to-end p95 at 1,000, 4,000 and 10,000-token prompts; TL Index sufficiency on service-level tasks
hypotheses.confirmedIf: Both met
hypotheses.refutedIf: Either fails: the 200 ms class moves to shorter replies or faster silicon

hypotheses.claim: H5. Units of 8 H100s scale linearly behind the prefix-aware Envoy
hypotheses.measurement: p95 end-to-end at one unit's load on one node and twice that load on two nodes
hypotheses.confirmedIf: p95 within 10% at twice the load
hypotheses.refutedIf: p95 rises more than 10%

hypotheses.claim: H6. Borrowing works: with one bucket idle, a busy bucket's sustainable rate rises at least 50% by borrowing the idle bucket's replicas, and the lender's p95 stays inside its promise once its own traffic returns
hypotheses.measurement: Sustainable requests per second of the busy bucket with and without borrowing; the lender's p95 during and after
hypotheses.confirmedIf: Rate up 50% or more and the lender's promise held
hypotheses.refutedIf: The lender's p95 breaks its promise

hypotheses.claim: H7. One 8x H100 node serves 1 million input tokens a minute of mixed 1,000 to 10,000-token traffic with 95% of fast calls inside their bucket's promise (bucketed picker)
hypotheses.measurement: Fast-class attainment at 1x in the proof kit's load stage (two TP4 replicas, public Gemma 4 31B stand-in)
hypotheses.confirmedIf: 95% or more
hypotheses.refutedIf: Under 95%

hypotheses.claim: H8. The bucketed picker beats round robin on fast-call attainment on the same traffic
hypotheses.measurement: Attainment points, bucketed minus round robin, at 1x
hypotheses.confirmedIf: 5 points or more
hypotheses.refutedIf: 0 points or less: plain load balancing is enough

hypotheses.claim: H9. A drafter we train on public data comes within 10% of the public drafter's mean accepted length (per route: Speculators EAGLE-3; in the full plan also Speculators DFlash and Model Optimizer EAGLE-3)
hypotheses.measurement: tau ours / tau public on the same held-out prompts
hypotheses.confirmedIf: 0.90 or more: the pipeline is ready for the Core
hypotheses.refutedIf: Under 0.75

hypotheses.claim: H10. Gemma 4 31B on 8x H100 returns 300 tokens in 200 ms at p95 (1,000-token prompt, one call); pre-registered expectation: refuted
hypotheses.measurement: p95 end to end in the proof grid
hypotheses.confirmedIf: 200 ms or less
hypotheses.refutedIf: Over 200 ms: the 200 ms class belongs on the small model

killSignals.signal: H1 and H2 both refute in the proof
killSignals.action: Stop building a GPU fast lane for the 27B; choose the 7B Core, shorter replies or faster silicon for the 200 ms class

Drafter refresh at each Core release: retrain every release, or check acceptance first and refresh (warm-started) only when a bucket falls below its promise? Recommendation: check first

Purpose, in order: show and tell what ThinkLatent's models and their use cases are doing at the Enterprise (adoption, centralisation); self-serve (evaluate a use case, pick a model, train, deploy, onboard, run and monitor in one place); AI runs it. The journey is one tab in the nav that guides each role to its next step and sends people into the command-centre pages. Portal direction. Why we build it: to express the collective intelligence of the organisation, at institution level, by embedding it in models, which no frontier lab offers; once embedded, teams use the models for new use cases, those generate interaction data and feedback, and the business intelligence compounds. The portal must let people see that compounding without being told. The portal is organised around models and use cases, not roles: the model is the core pillar (foundation model, domain model built from it, use case on top, with versions that move together); the only thing tied to people is membership of a use case, given by adding a company email; everything the Head sees is open to everyone, including a leaderboard of use cases by usage and value. Every number links to the page behind it. The prototype is the full requirement for the next year: build everything, do not cut for timeline or role; hiding comes later as an option. Each request and each call inside it is a signal to capture and show. This supersedes the role workspaces of D-219 to D-222 and the role lens in D-234

Built and published on D-236: role switch removed; a space for every use case with people, invite by company email and an open view for non-members; command-centre leaderboard open to everyone (tasks, share, paid, avoided by the Finance method, model, hosting, contact); model-to-use-case flows; catalogue of foundation models only, each model's page listing every use case on it and the versions trained from it; TL Index overview with every model's score, best model per pillar and a model picker; the loop page following one turn record by record; the signals page listing what one request gives and which signals are not captured yet; the data loop (new kinds of data found, feedback shared back). Sample records for these were added to the scenario package; the counts of new data examples and the feedback rate are sample anchors, not measurements. Not done: a value index across use cases (no formula agreed), the remaining role-shaped pages (approvals, operations) are open to all but still worded for their old owners

Portal direction, continued. (1) The TL Index is built inside the portal from now on, not beside it; it gets a preference rating from blind votes (an Elo-style score), on a page named Head to head, shown beside the Index score and never cited by an approval. (2) The Index gets a category, Real Enterprise, built from every use case's own items, with a score per use case; the team writes the items (the ask is in enterprise-benchmark-team-ask-2026-11-11.md). Public benchmark samples are adopted on day one as the format and a smoke test. (3) What the serving backend logs (traces, sessions, scores) comes into the portal in the portal's own design, at use-case level and rolled up at model level. (4) Beyond performance, the portal watches the data flow itself: requests by size (tokens in against tokens out), what requests are about, entities, their trend, and a Watch agent that flags what moved. (5) References for the Index pages: a public model leaderboard, its single-model page and its trends page (frontier, open and TLM side by side); the model page lists every use case row by row with live numbers.

Built and published on D-238: Traces (list and one page per request with its steps on the clock), Sessions (list and replay), Scores and review (score kinds, review queue), Flow watch (size map, answer-length spread, kinds of request by week, entities, Watch agent flags), the same rolled up on each model page with every use case as a row; Head to head with the preference rating. All of it is a seeded sample of 412 requests across six use cases; the Watch agent flags only changes it can tell from chance, and two of its three flags are changes written into the sample on purpose. Pilot and Production text is shown as sealed, which the backend does not yet enforce. Not built: the Index pages modelled on the public leaderboard, single-model and trends pages; the Real Enterprise category in the Index (the ask to the team is written, no items exist); agent graph; filters by tag, user and score. The word for a use case stays 'use case' on screen until Jithin confirms the rename to 'project'.

The form of every exhibit is chosen before it is built. Jithin called out that screens were being built from whatever was nearest to hand and that it is hurting the portal. A check (check:representation) counts hand-built tables, charts and pill navigation per file and fails if a count rises. Audit on the day: the portal used 5 of the kit's 64 base components and none of the 2,384 usable vendored ones, with 14 hand-built tables against 5 kit tables; 20 hand-built pieces remain after the observe and model pages moved to the kit table.

Scope and form of the portal build, after Jithin compared the prototype with the design canvas. (1) Nothing is removed: the build is every feature on the canvas plus every feature asked for in conversation; no feature leaves without a recorded decision. (2) Home is the canvas's Home (board H1) and is the same for everyone: what the Head of ThinkLatent sees is what anyone sees first. A person's own view moves to one clearly named tab (working name 'My work'). (3) The portal is a desktop application first: the layout follows the boards, with content beside the nav and filling the screen; the prototype's centred column with a gap is not the design. (4) A project proposal is written from every conversation and is the living requirement: executive summary, vision, feature list traced to the canvas, architecture, a five-year horizon with nothing held back, and three component alternatives for each section. The wireframe built from it is what the backend is built and connected to; what is switched on in the final product is decided after the wireframe exists.

Project proposal drafted (claude.ai document, linked from artifacts/TL-003-portal/project-proposal.pointer.md) with a feature register of 712 rows (artifacts/TL-003-portal/feature-register.md and project knowledge): 556 canvas features with ids by canvas page, 85 requirements that are not boards, 46 asked for in conversation, and 25 proposed by Claude for the five-year horizon (V rows, not asked for by Jithin, his to switch off). Findings recorded in it: the canvas audit of 10 Nov stands at 38 present, 150 partial, 361 missing and has not been recounted since; the prototype's content was capped at 1,240 px and centred, leaving about 300 px beside the nav on a wide screen; twelve first-pick components need design-kit wrappers that do not exist, and the step waterfall chart is new work. Eight decisions are put to Jithin in the proposal (tab name, 'Preview as', 'Project' or 'use case', value index, the Index's independence under D-155, a quote from the outside benchmark provider, which horizon proposals stay, component picks). Nothing was built or changed in the prototype in this session part.

Vision clarified in the build chat, one question at a time. It reaffirms D-236: models and projects, no roles; 'Preview as' and the role homes are not to be built (this reverses that part of D-248). (1) 'Model' means every kind of model, not only language models: TLM1-generation classifiers built on BERT, the speech-recognition network that processes about 150,000 calls a day, redaction, guardrails, embeddings, rerankers (Claude's reading of 'reversion model', not yet confirmed), and models that work in the background; more as applications evolve. (2) Many to many: a model serves many projects and one project uses several models, as different jobs in one flow, as separate features, as old and new side by side, and as agents that bring a model. (3) The project carries the stage and is delivered in increments: new models for new tasks are added at any time, increments run in parallel, and each goes to production on its own approval. (4) Each kind of model is scored on its own measure with a bar and a leaderboard of its kind; the TL Index stays for language models. (5) A shared model is handled both ways: Enterprise-wide work is one project for the Enterprise, and the same model can also sit inside another project for its own purpose (speech in an application's interface, redaction as a support function). (6) Hierarchy, in Jithin's words: Organization, Team, Project, Feature (for example Retail Business, Advice Tech, Advisor desktop, then call summary, next best action, speech to text; the same team can hold a second project), with models under features. The names and where membership sits are still being settled. Where a board assumes roles or one model per project, this vision wins and the board guides layout only (amends D-247).

Vision, continued (follows D-249). (1) Levels: Organization, Team, Project, Feature, with models under features; a project carries its team as owner and can move teams without losing its history (Claude's caution, not yet confirmed). (2) Membership: people join a project; a team's owners can open and manage every project the team holds; everyone else gets the open view. (3) Rule for the whole navigation: every level shows the breakdown of the level below it, and the detail (traces, sessions, operations) lives at the project; a model's page shows improvement, API calls and tokens, adoption and value. (4) Two-level navigation, option A, chosen from three drawn options (canvas 'navigation options'): the approved dock stays and gets shorter; a clickable scope bar says where you are (Organization, Team, Project, Feature); tabs under the title change with the level. (5) Home is a cockpit, not one list: TLM model adoption and what is running in production today by stage; usage by kind; an adoption and usage leaderboard at team level with a double-click into a team's projects; and the AI agent in front, which understands the ask, brings the information and routes the person to the right place, flattening the path from onboarding to approvals. (6) Jithin's ask for what follows: Claude keeps asking questions one at a time until the vision is clear, then designs the UX and UI in the approved design and draws it by hand so it fits; nothing more is built until then.

Vision, continued (follows D-250). (1) Usage by kind of work comes off Home for now and is parked for later as a Home exhibit; Home keeps models live by kind and requests split into live and background. (2) Approvals sit outside the portal, for projects and for models alike. A deployment triggers a workflow in the Enterprise's change system and the change request is approved by the ThinkLatent team; model approval is also recorded in an outside system. The portal prepares the evidence, raises the request and shows its status; it approves nothing. The approver queues and hold-to-approve screens for use cases and validations on the earlier boards become request status. (3) The model catalogue is grouped by generation first (TLM1 to TLM5), with the kinds of model inside each. (4) Budgets are held by the team; spend and value are counted per project and feature and roll up to team and organization. (5) Taken as settled unless Jithin says otherwise: the agent on Home is one line at the top of the cockpit (Claude's recommendation after Jithin asked for analysis); 'reversion model' is read as reranker.

On the first draft of the Home cockpit ('looks good', with three changes). (1) No budgets in the portal: budget detail will not be available, so the portal shows spend and what was saved, meaning cost avoided for the company; this reverses item 4 of D-251. (2) The flow from models to teams leaves Home: it is good but falls apart beyond about ten models; the space becomes a quick model catalogue, tiles that open each model's page, with what is new and coming (releases, retraining, editions) beside it. The mapping of models to teams and projects stays on each model's and each team's page. (3) Tokens are the common unit across every kind of model, speech included: input and output tokens are shown for each model, and the overall tokens in and out sit at the title level of Home to show the scale. Second draft drawn with these on the canvas.

The second draft of the Home cockpit is accepted ('looking good, continue'): the agent line, running now, a quick model catalogue with what is new and coming, teams ranked by adoption with spend and cost avoided, and tokens in and out at the title and on each model. Claude continues drawing the rest of the structure on the canvas in the same way, one screen at a time: a model's page is drafted next (scope bar All models, generation, model, version; its measure, adoption, improvement by version, what it is built from, where it is used with its job in each feature, tokens by day).

Four more libraries go into the kit as owned source on kit tokens, so every product can use and change them freely: Beautiful UI (MIT, from a public mirror of the site's code), Bencho's free blocks (MIT), BoardUI's free set (MIT, kept on React Aria, Remix icons swapped for Lucide) and the 36 free Transitions.dev transitions. Transitions.dev has a custom licence that forbids republishing the collection as a kit: allowed as a recorded exception on the condition that the kit stays private and is never published, sold or given away, its comment stays on each transition, and no Pro transitions are taken. Paid tiers of Bencho, BoardUI and Transitions.dev are not taken. design-kit v0.8.0 (cdebcec): 2,514 of 2,539 usable, 25 excluded, none blocked

The first draft of a model's page is accepted ('continue, it looks good'). Drawn next on the same canvas, for his review: a project's page (Advisor desktop: scope bar organization, team, project, feature; its features with the models in each in the order they run, tokens and score against its bar per feature; increments with the status of each change request, approved outside the portal; members; traces, sessions and operations at project level) and the Models catalogue by generation (TLM5 to TLM1, kinds inside, one row a model with its version and state, its own measure against its bar, where it is used, calls and tokens in and out). Sample totals now add up across the boards: 2.3B tokens in, 208M out across nine live models. Open with Jithin: what TLM2 held, and whether the split of kinds across generations is right.

The libraries added in v0.8.0 are made usable by products through a library layer in @kit/kit (one kit-owned import path per usable component: agent 19, interactions 47, controls 64) and by giving 29 sample-content components real data props in the owned source; 93 of 130 now take real data, the other 37 are flagged as sample-only. Tried in a copy of the portal with portal-style data: its type check, usable check and build pass. design-kit v0.9.0 (e2a4cac)

Before any more design, the portal moves to the latest design kit: pin e2a4cac (v0.9.0), pulled with its motion package, with the two library aliases, the six packages and the two stylesheets the kit asks for (portal 7bd63d2). No screen changed: twenty pages were compared pixel for pixel with the previous build, in light, dark and on a phone, and one demo date was crawled at both widths. The portal's rules now say: library components come from @kit/kit/library, only those marked as taking real data, always with their content passed; controls stay on @kit/ui where it has them; charts stay on @kit/charts. Eleven library components were tried with the drawn pages' content: task rows fit a project's increments, the filter table fits requests and their status, the recommendation card fits the agent's answer to 'find a model for a task', tool chips fit a trace; the stat cards, records table and chart-like pieces are not used. The drawn pages keep their layout and look; these four pieces are redrawn with the new components. Cost to note: the build's styles grew from 0.56 MB to 1.94 MB with no library component on a page yet.

The generations in the catalogue are as Jithin states them: TLM1 the task models; TLM2 and TLM3 language models; TLM4 the current language models on a new open-source base, with the domain models and the decision models; TLM5 a large world model. The catalogue is redrawn to this: TLM4 holds Core, Distil, Domain and Decision as its kinds; the guardrail that runs in the background sits with the TLM1 task models (Claude's reading, to be confirmed); a version trained for one project is not a catalogue row and shows on its base model instead; eight models live in the sample. The project page's increments are redrawn as task rows and a team's page is drafted (projects with the stage each carries, the models the team uses with their job in each project, increments in flight, owners). Jithin also set the working method for the rest of the design: keep asking one question at a time and redrawing the pages until every page is done.

The page that replaces approvals, 'Requests and their status', tracks four kinds of request on one page: deployment change requests (an increment going to Pilot or Production, decided in the Enterprise's change system by the ThinkLatent team), access requests (joining a project is settled by its owners in the portal; production access is granted in IAM), asks to ThinkLatent (a new project, a new model or feature, training capacity) and problems logged (each a ticket, listed openly). The page is drafted: a card per kind saying where it is decided, and one list filtered by where a request stands (needs you, waiting on others, being prepared). The portal prepares, raises and shows status; it approves nothing.

A feature has two bars: a minimum set by the ThinkLatent team for each kind of task (as the 85% safety minimum already is, on every feature), and the project team's own target above it. A feature's page is drafted on this (Call summary): its score by week against both bars, the bars by measure, how a request runs through its models with what each processed, what advisors say, and its increments; its traces open in the project. The project page shows both bars per feature. Proposed by Claude and still to be confirmed: a change request cannot be raised while a score is under its minimum, and can be raised with a note when it is only under the team's target. Jithin also asked that questions come through the question prompt, with a recommendation, so that he is notified.

What a feature is held to is two kinds of bar on two different measures, corrected by Jithin. The TL Index thresholds come from the ThinkLatent team, because the project uses a model from ThinkLatent's list that is already scored on the Index. The project team sets what it expects of the application's own quality. After training, the project team may go ahead under a TL Index threshold: that is a risk the team accepts, it is flagged on the feature and the project, and the deviation travels with the evidence so that governance, which approves outside the portal, sees it. Claude's earlier line that a change request cannot be raised under a minimum is withdrawn. For application quality the portal gives teams default ways of scoring to choose from (exact match, F1 score, closeness to a reference, a model as judge with standard judges, a model as judge with the team's own rubric, people scoring a sample) and one data format their evaluation set must match, with a template and a check on every upload. The feature page is redrawn to this and a feature's evaluation set page is drafted; the field names in the format are Claude's proposal for the team to confirm.

Two more answers. A project team's own judge must be checked against answers the team scored by hand before its scores count as evidence, and the agreement is shown with the evidence. The guided next step lives in the project and is listed in My work; there is no separate Journey item in the dock, and the agent can walk a person through any step. My work is drafted on this, with no roles: a short account from the agent of what changed since the person was last here, the next step in each of their projects with the project's stage, the requests that need them and those they wait on, what they follow, and what they opened recently. Nothing lives only on My work.

The journey is a plan that everyone sees from the first day, the ThinkLatent team included: every phase from set up to production, what each party owes in it, the least a team needs to move forward, and the things with a long lead time that delay the date when the team does not say early (machines to reserve, GPU or CPU, a dedicated or shared endpoint, service levels to agree, the time governance needs to evaluate). It is drawn as a Plan page on the project: four asks with their lead time and last safe day, a phase-by-party plan (project team, ThinkLatent team, infrastructure, governance outside the portal), the least needed to move to the next phase, and what moves the date, with the team's target beside the earliest date the plan allows. The lead times shown are sample values for ThinkLatent to replace. Also drawn: the page of a task model, Speech recognition, with word error rate by version and by business line, since that is how it runs today. Jithin asked that anything Claude needs from him comes as a question with a recommendation to select.

Who is on a project's plan. Hosting the model is ThinkLatent's own work, so there is no separate infrastructure party. ThinkLatent appears as two teams: product and adoption (client-facing: what a team needs to adopt a model, its guide through the plan) and AI engineering (the models, the machines and the endpoints), with one ThinkLatent lead assigned to the project for model and infrastructure matters. Connecting the application is system integration, and the project team should name a dedicated integration lead for it. The Plan page is redrawn with five lanes: project team, integration lead, ThinkLatent product, ThinkLatent AI engineering, governance outside the portal, and the named leads on top. Also settled: the lead times on the plan stay as sample values for the ThinkLatent team to fill; the background guardrail is a TLM1 task model today and a TLM4 Judge takes it over later; the reranker is dropped for now, from the catalogue and from the sample flows (ten models in the sample, eight live).

Four more answers. The five phases keep their names and each says what it delivers (Try: evaluation and proof it works; Build: integration, training if needed). A deployment's change request is approved by ThinkLatent's AI engineering team, outside the portal. Joining a project is settled by the project's owners in the portal, and the ThinkLatent team can see the ask; every project gets a ThinkLatent point of contact assigned automatically, alongside the portal's AI guide. The guide has no settled name and is called Jarvis for now. Jithin left 'what to draw next' open, so Claude took its recommended option and drew starting a project with Jarvis: a conversation that asks only what the plan needs, suggests models from the catalogue, fills the project in beside the conversation, shows the dates the answers give, and can open the project as soon as the least is known, with open answers shown as dates at risk.

Traces and sessions. For now everything in a trace is visible in the portal, text included, behind one switch that seals the text; later the switch goes away and IAM roles decide, once Jithin has agreed the roles with governance (this replaces sealing Pilot and Production text on every screen as the working rule, and closes the open sealing decision due 18 Nov). The trace and the session are to be specified in full detail as the requirement the ThinkLatent AI engineering team builds to, for the five-year vision, with nothing held back: every page's numbers broken down to the request; what vLLM and its OpenAI-compatible API give; what must be added in the background (guardrail, sensitive-data exposure, entities, classification, whether the request is of a kind seen in training); and thumbs for a turn and for a session sent back by the application. Written as 'Trace and session requirement v1' (about 190 fields in thirteen groups, each with its level, its source and whether the seal hides it; how every page's numbers come from them; what to add to the team's Langfuse schema), from the vLLM, Langfuse and OpenTelemetry documentation. Drawn (first drafts, with Jithin for review): the Agents shelf, with three agents ready on an official score, one offered by a team and being scored, three in build and 34 planned with their asks, and how a team offers an agent; an agent's page (Policy Q&A agent), with its measures, the same task built three ways beside an outside model, how a task runs, what the agent may and may not do, who uses it, its versions and how to adopt it through one endpoint; and Agents at work, the portal's own five agents with what each did, what waits for a person, the accepted share, what an agent may do and the record of pauses. Agent chips on the boards and a chip on Home open Agents at work; the catalogue's tab row opens the shelf. Claude's reading, flagged: an agent differs from a system of models in that it takes steps and may use tools, and is otherwise picked, tried, called and scored the same way; the portal's agents still only propose, with pre-agreed reversible steps shown as planned. Also fixed: ThinkLatent's thresholds for Call summary now read '2 of 3 met, 1 accepted' on Quality, the feature page and the open view.

Jithin moved on from the three agent boards without changes ('continue, let's move forward'). Operations in depth is taken in four parts: alerts and incidents, rollout and serving, operations across the Enterprise, the audit trail. On the first part his four answers: alerts and incidents live inside a project's Operations tab; ThinkLatent's on-call acts on every alert, service or quality, and brings the project in when needed, the project being told at each step; the Enterprise's own incident and paging tool calls people and keeps the record, while the portal raises the alert into it, shows where the incident stands and adds its own timeline and the SRE agent's draft review; and an alert fires only from what is already agreed (a service level broken, a score under the floor of its range) or from a change the SRE agent sees that chance is unlikely to explain, so nobody writes a rule. It follows that team-written alert rules, the escalation chain with quiet hours, and acknowledging or silencing an alert in the portal leave the feature list by this decision (C-p6-35 to C-p6-37); they belong to the Enterprise's tool. Drawn (first drafts, with Jithin for review): a section 'Alerts and incidents' on Operations (no alert open, who is on call, what can fire, and the last 30 days: two changes the SRE agent noticed and one incident), and an incident's page for 20 Oct, when Call summary did not answer for 11 minutes: five numbers, requests minute by minute, the timeline of who did what, the SRE agent's review signed by ThinkLatent's on-call, and the incident as it stands in the Enterprise's tool. The sample agrees with the service levels already drawn (99.93% up and 0.15% of requests failing over 30 days) and with problem PR-0058.

Jithin moved on from alerts and incidents without changes ('continue') and took the second part of operations, rollout and serving. His four answers: a rollout lives in Increments, as the last step of an increment, and the serving set-up lives on Operations; a rollout moves itself (its steps are fixed when the change is approved, it goes on while the watched numbers hold, waits when it cannot tell yet and goes back by itself if one is clearly worse), and an owner or ThinkLatent's on-call can hold it or take it back at any time with no approval; every rollout begins with a silent step of about a day, where the new version answers a copy of live requests and nobody sees its answers; and a smaller, cheaper model that still clears a feature's measures is offered to a project as a new version is, with the project's own results already run, the owner deciding, and the switch travelling as an increment, so five things can now start an increment. Drawn (first drafts, with Jithin for review): a rollout's page (the record of Call summary moving to version 2 on 2 to 5 Oct: four steps and who met the new version at each, version 1 against version 2 on five watched numbers with the call at each step, what happened, the way back, and what was fixed at approval); the Index agent's offer of the small Core for the wording step of Next best action (what would change, the project's own measures side by side, speed, cost and room, what the project would give up, and what follows either answer); and 'How it is served' on Operations (what the project chose, what ThinkLatent set, what is ahead, and asking for more room for a period). The Increments board, the Overview and the new-version offer now describe the same rollout; increment 3's approval reads 2 Oct so its three-day rollout ends on 5 Oct; an old version stays ready 90 days everywhere (D-282). Not drawn yet from this part: the engine's own settings and counters behind the Engineering switch, and routing by task.

Jithin moved on from rollout and serving without changes ('ok, let's continue') and took the third part of operations, the view across the Enterprise. His three answers: everyone at the Enterprise sees the page (health, room and what is coming) and only ThinkLatent sees the engine detail and can move or release machines; the machines held by training show as a total only, with when they free up and no model or run named, so the rule that nobody outside the foundation team sees a training run until release holds; and three older features leave the feature list: unregistered keys and applications (C-p12-01 to C-p12-03), calls missing their tags (C-p12-04, C-p3-52) with the key register (C-p3-51, already empty since D-287), and the view of teams calling outside vendors directly (C-p12-05), which belongs to AI governance's list of approved tools. This also confirms the rule assumed in D-286: a call with a missing or unknown project or feature id is refused at once. Drawn (first draft, with Jithin for review): Operations across the Enterprise, behind Home's 'Requests today': five numbers; all ten endpoints, the tightest first, each with who it serves, its machines, how busy it is at the peak against the 15% of room ThinkLatent aims to keep, its service levels and what to know; the 46 machines as serving, testing, training and free, with 4 on order; what the next six weeks need against the machines there are; use by team; and what ThinkLatent can do on the page, with one proposal from the SRE agent. A system of models is one endpoint to its project and several rows here. The sample now counts ten endpoints everywhere (the Value page and Agents at work said nine). Still assumed from D-286: limits apply on shared endpoints only.

Jithin moved on from operations across the Enterprise without changes ('ok continue') and took the fourth and last part of operations, the audit trail. His three answers: the record lives only inside each project, as the Members tab's log grown into the full record, with no view across projects (Claude had recommended one page scoped to where it is opened); decisions are open to everyone at the Enterprise, while lines about who opened sealed production text show only to the project's members, ThinkLatent and auditors; and the Enterprise's Risk and Audit people read through a read-only role granted in IAM, which reads every project's record one project at a time and never the text, with export beside it (an owner exports their own project, ThinkLatent and auditors any, as a file that expires). Drawn (first draft, with Jithin for review): a project's record, opened from 'The whole record' on Members: five numbers for the last 30 days; every line newest first with who, what, why or what it rests on and one of six kinds (decision, sealed text opened, agent proposed, from outside, members, access), the sealed-text lines shaded as restricted; who can read what; production access for a period (one ask waiting in IAM, one used on 28 Oct); and export. A line cannot be changed or removed; taking something back is a new line; looking at a page is not recorded, opening sealed text and exporting are. The review of access grants stays with the Enterprise's own access review, in line with D-284. How long the record is kept follows the Enterprise's records policy and is not yet known. With this, operations in depth is drawn in all four parts. Also corrected: the SRE agent's finding of 3 Nov joined problem PR-0077, which was logged on 2 Nov, on Agents at work and Operations.

Jithin moved on from the record without changes ('continue') and took the foundation team's side, in three parts: data work, training beyond a single run, prompts. On data work his three answers: it lives in a Data tab in Models and agents that only the foundation team and the reviewers it names see, by IAM; for the foundation team the data can be visible in the portal, because they are the ThinkLatent team that curates data for training and for evaluation, making the TL Index stronger, and reviews it (Claude had recommended showing only the flag); and when a source withdraws data, each run and model trained on it is flagged and a person, the foundation lead, decides whether to retrain. This narrows the standing rule: no row of a data set is visible to anyone outside the foundation team, anywhere in the portal; inside the Data tab that team reads rows, and every opening is recorded. Drawn (first drafts, with Jithin for review): the Data tab (five numbers; reviews waiting by why an item was flagged; four tagging pipelines with the share of their flags that reviews found right, one running silently; the nine data sets, five for training and four for evaluation, with versions, source, counts and where each was used); reviewing one flagged item (the redacted record with the flagged words marked, why it is there, similar items decided, a two-question decision with a reason, and what the decision does); and one data set's page (a withdrawal of 412 calls waiting for the foundation lead with three ways to answer, its versions, checks, where it went, and how it is kept). The training board now says rows are read only in the Data tab. Claude's reading, to confirm: examples brought back from self-healing, redacted before they arrive, are readable by the foundation team like any other set. Not drawn yet from data work: the reviewers' table and second reviews in detail, tuning a pipeline's level against past reviews, pipeline proposals, the knowledge graph's status and topic coverage, comparing two versions.

Jithin set the frame for the foundation team's data and training, answered four questions on it, and asked for research on the NVIDIA NeMo stack before more is drawn. The frame: an item of training data is tagged by the kinds of training it can serve (supervised fine-tuning, RLHF, RLAIF, distillation), by TL Index pillar and by category (financial, general, regulatory, LM safety, cyber attack); a knowledge graph in the backend, built from that metadata, selects sources on disk for training, sampling and whatever else a pipeline needs; the Training tab is designed ahead of what exists, across every training method and data-pipeline need; the training code is on the NVIDIA NeMo ecosystem; and pruning is the first step for a base model, which is pruned to align with the Enterprise's data so that it is ready for that data before the later stages. His four answers: tags are set by pipelines and checked by people, who review low-confidence items and a sample of every version; LM safety and cyber attack data is open to the whole foundation team with no limit on what it may train (Claude had recommended a named few and defence-only use); recipes are built in the portal, stages and methods assembled without code (Claude had recommended picking a recipe kept as reviewed code); and examples brought back from self-healing are readable by the foundation team under the same rule as every other data set, which closes the reading left open in D-294. Claude's working assumptions, put to him and not contested: a mix is a saved, versioned selection; a judge that trains a model never scores it on the TL Index; tasks, checks and judges sit on a second shelf in the Data tab; every method is shown as Ready, In build or Planned. Written: a scout brief on the NeMo stack, in project knowledge and the repository. It finds that the original NeMo repository is now speech only and its language-model collection deprecated; recommends Megatron-Bridge with Model Optimizer for shaping the base (adjust the full base, prune, distil back), AutoModel for fine-tuning, NeMo RL and NeMo Gym for the preference and reinforcement stages, Curator and Data Designer for data, Evaluator beside the TL Index, and NVIDIA's Nemotron recipes as the reference for chains of stages; and names one check before relying on it: whether the pruning path covers the Gemma 4 base that Core uses. Nothing was drawn in this step; the Data and Training boards follow.

Jithin corrected the scout brief on the NVIDIA NeMo stack: the team decided not to use Megatron-Bridge during training and has been executing without it, because the TLM bases are Gemma and Phi. This overturns the brief's recommendation in D-295 to shape the base on Megatron-Bridge with Model Optimizer. The brief is revised (version 2, in project knowledge and the repository): AutoModel is the training spine (the light fine-tune before pruning, distilling back after it, fine-tuning and adapters), NeMo RL runs on its PyTorch-native backend with NeMo Gym for the preference and reinforcement stages, Curator and Data Designer serve data, Evaluator sits beside the TL Index, Model Optimizer is used for quantisation, and pruning stays the TLM package's own code, since NVIDIA's documented language-model pruning runs on the Megatron side. The reading supports the team's choice: the bridge's list of supported families has no Phi and its dense Gemma 4 support was incomplete, and staying on Hugging Face checkpoints keeps every model in the format vLLM serves. The order of stages stands, with pruning first inside 'shape the base' (adjust the full base, prune, distil back). The Gemma 4 check asked for in D-295 is withdrawn; in its place the foundation lead is asked which pruning method and settings the TLM package exposes, so that the recipe builder's Prune stage shows the right ones. Nothing was drawn in this step.

Reading the scout brief on the NVIDIA NeMo stack, Jithin marked two rows: NeMo Skills is to be considered (Claude had it as later), and NeMo-Run is to be considered. He also reported that the team has made Gemma 4 work on its own training path, the dense model specifically, which removes the risk the brief had named around dense Gemma 4. The brief is revised to version 3 with both verdicts and that fact. Nothing was drawn in this step.

Jithin gave the go to draw ('we are good to go'): redraw the Data tab and draw Training, with 'Shape the base' (adjust, prune, distil back) as the first block of every base recipe. Drawn, as first drafts with Jithin for review. The Data tab, second draft: six numbers; what the store can train as a table of use by category (plain text, examples with a checked answer, pairs picked by people, pairs picked by a judge, a stronger model's answers, classifier labels, tasks with a check, evaluation only, against financial, general, regulatory, LM safety and cyber attack), with cells marked thin against what saved recipes ask for; the same by TL Index pillar; the 16 data sets, 12 for training and 4 for evaluation, each with its tags, source and rights; a second shelf for tasks with a check, judges for training and reward models, with the rule that a judge that helps train a model never scores it on the TL Index; and how it is held, with rows on disk and only tags and links in the graph. Tags and reviews: the seven kinds of tag (what it can train, TL Index pillar, category, source and rights, sensitivity, who checked it, shape), who or what sets each and how often it is found right; the review queue, now with tags a pipeline was not sure of and samples of a judge's picks; eight tagging pipelines; and what a correction does. A mix: the ask in words and in tags, what the graph found by data set, the mix by TL Index pillar against what the recipe asks for, the checks on it, how it is drawn (order, replay, weight, cap, held out, seed), where it sits and the six saved mixes, two of them for shaping a base. Training, a new tab beside Data for the foundation team: four recipes as chains of stages, the 22 methods grouped by what they learn from, each with what it needs from the store, how much is held, what it is built on and whether it is ready, in build or planned, and the runs. A recipe built in the portal: a base from a new open model, seven stages with 'Shape the base' outlined and first, the settings the Prune stage exposes, what a stage needs and whether the store has it, the checks before it starts, and running it. LM safety and cyber attack data is drawn as he chose, open to the whole team and to any mix, with its share shown on every mix and recipe. Built-on names follow D-296 and D-297: AutoModel, the TLM package for pruning, NeMo RL and NeMo Gym, Model Optimizer for quantising. The canvas has 56 boards, every one reachable and no broken link. Sample values that are guesses until the team confirms: the pruning settings, each method's status, and what each method is built on.

Jithin answered four questions on training beyond a single run. On pruning, in his own words: width is what the team does now, with FastNAS as he recalls it, and it can be researched and made better; 5% and 10% have been taken out so far, the team needs to reach 20%, and a good evaluation will help to quantify it. A recipe's training shows as one run with its stages inside. When a stage's check fails the run stops and a person decides. The portal proposes the checkpoint that goes forward and the foundation lead decides. Drawn, as first drafts with Jithin for review: every run, with two ticked and compared (the 10% and 20% shaping trials: what differed, what it bought in size and speed, and the points lost on each TL Index pillar against the adjusted full base, as differences with their ranges against the 2 points allowed); and one run with its stages inside (the 20% trial stopped at stage 3's check, the check by pillar, what happens next as a proposal with three choices for the foundation lead, stage 3's checkpoints with the one the portal proposes, what the run used, and the path from a run to a release). The recipe's Prune stage is redrawn as the team runs it: FastNAS from Model Optimizer, width only, 20% as the aim with 5% and 10% run, and the note that the ranking score is what the method searches on, so a better evaluation makes a better cut. The scout brief is at version 4: Model Optimizer documents FastNAS as its mode for vision models and GradNAS as its mode for Hugging Face language models, with Puzzletron taking GradNAS's place in its newer documentation, so the brief asks for one trial each against FastNAS; it also says how to quantify a cut (the whole Index, question by question against the adjusted full base, with a range) and to try 15% and a longer distilling back before concluding on 20%. Claude's assumptions on the boards, to confirm: a stage's check is scored on the whole TL Index on the same questions as the base; checkpoints other than the proposed one and each stage's last are removed after 30 days; the method named is as Jithin recalls it. The canvas has 58 boards.

Jithin answered four questions on prompts. A feature's prompt versions live on the feature, with a library of templates in Models and agents. The application holds the prompt text and the portal registers each version (Claude had recommended that the portal hold the text and the application send an id). A new prompt version reaches production as an increment, with the same rollout as everything else. Of the eight checks on a version, two block (a secret in the text, a client's name or account in the examples) and six warn. Drawn, as first drafts with Jithin for review. A Prompts tab on the feature's page: the share of calls carrying a registered version; the versions with who registered each, from which application release, what changed, where it stands and its score; two versions compared (the change in the text, shown to members only, and what it does to the feature's measures as differences with their ranges, to length, time and cost at all of today's traffic); the eight checks; practice before an increment, on the evaluation set and silently on copies of yesterday's requests; how each version reached production; a wording proposed by self-healing for the next version; and what is watched (calls with no registered version, a version in production that was never practised, production moving outside an increment). A prompt library, a tab in Models and agents open to everyone: 14 templates with what each is for, the model it is written for, its TL Index pillar, the features started from it and its checks; one template opened; who started from it and how far behind each is; and how starting from, following and offering a template work. A new version of a prompt is now a sixth way to start an increment, and the catalogue's tab row gains Prompts. This covers the feature rows C-p6-01 to C-p6-12. What follows from the application holding the text, shown on the board: the application moves the traffic at each step of a rollout, the portal watches and tells the owner and ThinkLatent's on-call when to hold or go back, and the portal cannot take a prompt back by itself. Claude's readings, to confirm: registering a version sends its text to the portal, which is what lets the checks and the comparison run; the text shows only to the project's members and the two ThinkLatent people on it; a team's template joins the library once ThinkLatent has run the checks and scored it, as with agents. The canvas has 60 boards.

Jithin asked that Claude put its assumptions to him as questions with a recommendation, not assume, so that both are on the same page; twelve were asked and answered. On prompts: registering a version sends its text to the portal, where the project's members can read it; a team's prompt joins the library after ThinkLatent has checked and scored it. On training: a stage's check is scored on the whole TL Index; a base may lose 2 points on any live pillar before a run stops; two checkpoints are kept for each stage, the best and the last, in place of Claude's rule of keeping others for 30 days; a judge used in training may also score a model on the TL Index, where Claude had drawn a rule against it (the rule and its checks are removed from the boards); the Data tab becomes four pages, with the data sets on their own. On where a run lives, in his words: training runs as Slurm jobs on HyperPod, a dedicated S3 bucket holds the runs, each under a run id; during training things are brought into the FSx area of the cluster for fast access, and a checkpoint that beats the best is written to the run's S3 prefix, so that lineage, the data used and the configuration are all in the run's folder; a model good enough for consumption is promoted to a standard place. He chose pointers to the data, not copies, and asked what happens if the store changes during a run: versions never change once cut, a run trains on the copy it took at its start, and for the one real change, a withdrawal, the run finishes and the foundation lead then decides. Release is one step: once the TL Index run confirms the model works it is released, the projects on it are told, and the portal runs each project's own evaluation ahead of them so the team can decide; this puts release before the projects' evaluations, where the boards had them the other way round. Recipes are kept in the portal, with standard recipes defined by ThinkLatent at the start and new ones built from the methods available; a run freezes its recipe into its folder (this replaces 'a file in the TLM package'). A run's folder is kept 180 days after the run ends, and the small record of a run that produced a released model travels with the model. A run's id is readable and meaningful: model, what the run is for (the project where there is one) and date; Claude set the form as model, purpose, date and a letter. Written: a requirement for AI engineering, 'Training runs: where a run lives, the process and the folder for each run id' (the four places, the run id, the folder tree, the FSx layout, the released model's folder, twelve steps with who writes what, what happens if data changes, what is kept, and five open choices each with a recommendation). Drawn or changed: a run's files (new), the data sets on their own page (new), the run page (two checkpoints, the path to a release in the new order), the recipe and Training pages (standard recipes, kept in the portal), the model's own Training page (release order), the Data pages (no judge rule, four pages). Sample dates on this stretch's boards were also moved to fit the boards' own clock of 5 Nov, and Core's run 6 was corrected to the released 4.2. The canvas has 62 boards.

Twelve more points settled by question on 13 Nov, eleven as recommended. Reuse of training work: a checkpoint is kept while any run uses it; what is valuable and works is released and then follows the released lifecycle; a run reuses work only from a released item or an active run, where active means going or ended inside its 180 days, and only a stage that passed its check can be reused. A shaped or adjusted base that works is released to a base shelf beside the models, seen by the foundation team only, never in the catalogue, and kept while any model built on it is kept. Limits apply on shared endpoints only (confirmed). A system of models gets one catalogue page with its own score and thresholds, the models inside shown to ThinkLatent only (to be drawn with the models theme). A project's record is kept for the project's life and then for the period the Enterprise's records rule sets, with the period shown on the page. Registering the application is the project's engineers' step on the Plan, with AI engineering as help. TL Index upkeep: a new edition each month, signed off by the Head of ThinkLatent; a sixth of each edition is new (200 questions) and 1,000 are carried; stage checks in training use their own set of 1,200 questions from the pool that are never in an edition, so that a checkpoint is never picked on the questions that later grade the model (this replaces 'the whole TL Index' for stage checks in D-301); anyone may ask for a model to be scored and ThinkLatent accepts, in the order release first, re-scoring after a correction, accepted asks by age, practice runs when machines are free, with a training run's checks shown to the foundation team only. Against the recommendation: only the team and the questions' writers may raise a correction to a question, with no flags from outside; corrections are still listed openly. Changed or drawn: the base shelf on Training; the run, run files, runs, recipe and a model's Training page (reuse, the base shelf, the stage-check set); the record ('How long the record is kept'); the Plan and Connect (registration). Requirements updated: training run storage v1.1; model training and release v1.1, brought in line with the release order of D-301. The canvas has 62 boards, split the same evening into eight pages by theme (Home, Models, TL Index, Agents and prompts, Data and training, A project, Features and increments, Traces and operations) after Jithin reported that the web page crashed while opening it.

Jithin on corrections to the TL Index, 13 Nov: only the ThinkLatent team corrects a question; a correction is made at once, as a new version that the record reflects; and the run that scores models again is held every two weeks, so that it is iterative and predictable (this narrows D-302, where the questions' writers could also raise one). Drawn on that reading: scores change only every second Tuesday, the four-weekly edition being every other one of those days (27 Oct edition 2026-11, 10 Nov corrections run, 24 Nov edition 2026-12). Three further questions went unanswered and Claude drew its recommendation for each, to be confirmed: a question that leaves an edition goes into the stage-check set and is then retired, one way only; the upkeep page is for ThinkLatent only, with the edition's page and the queue open to everyone; outside models are scored again with every edition and at once when a vendor changes a model. Drawn (first drafts): TL Index upkeep (the pool by pillar, a question's life, the next edition step by step, corrections), an edition's open page (models against the last edition on the carried questions, what changed, how it was signed off, the open list of corrections, the editions), and the evaluation queue (the order, what runs and waits, one run live with provisional scores, who sees what). The Data pages gained the Entity recognition evaluation set they lacked: 17 data sets, 5 for evaluation, 4,500 TL Index questions and 500 head-to-head pairs. The canvas has 65 boards on eight pages.

Four more answers on the TL Index, 13 Nov. Against the recommendation: a new edition every two weeks, not every four, with 100 new questions each time (20 a pillar) and corrections going in with it; the Head of ThinkLatent signs each one, so twice a month (this replaces the monthly edition with a sixth new in D-302 and the separate corrections run drawn in D-303). As recommended: a training run's check shows in the open queue as a nameless 'ThinkLatent · internal run'; a project may offer a version of its own evaluation set to the Index, which is profiled by the portal, checked blind by practitioners and accepted or declined by the pillar council, with the contributor credited and its own model never scored on what it gave; and no quote is asked from the outside benchmark company for now, its free public samples being run only as a smoke test. Claude named the second edition of a month with a letter (2026-11b on 10 Nov). Drawn or changed: upkeep, the edition's page and the queue reworked for two-weekly editions; the sign-off as the Head sees it while it waits, on upkeep; a set offered by a project (the offer, the profile's nine checks, the practitioner check, the proposal for the council, offers so far), reached from a feature's evaluation set. One consequence drawn rather than decided: real calls may not be sent to outside models, so the Index agent proposes a cap of 5 such questions among an edition's 20 new ones. The canvas has 66 boards.

Jithin on the TL Index, 13 Nov evening: a dedicated team keeps the Index from going stale, adding new questions and making the corrections, and he has that team, so its make-up is not a design question; corrections on a two-week or a monthly cycle are both fine (the two-weekly edition of D-304 stays as drawn); and at each edition only the new or corrected questions are measured again, the overall score being worked out by a delta calculation. He also asked Claude to remember to ask questions directly, each with a recommendation, so that work continues (saved to the Project's memory). Drawn or changed: upkeep, the edition's page and the queue now name the Index team and show delta scoring (a model answers only what changed; a changed model, ours or a vendor's, gets a full run); a Trends page (the best outside, ThinkLatent and open model over 13 editions, whether each pillar still tells models apart, the forecast, the quarterly report). Seven points he did not answer are drawn on Claude's recommendation and stay open for him: a question leaving an edition goes to the stage-check set and then retires; the upkeep page is ThinkLatent only; at most 5 real calls among an edition's 20 new questions; the Index team and the foundation team may both open a question (Claude recommends the Index team only); the Index agent watches saturation and the Index team hardens, with retiring a pillar left to the pillar council; trends are open and the forecast shows to ThinkLatent only; the quarterly report is drafted by the Index agent and signed by the Head. The canvas has 67 boards.

Eleven answers on the TL Index, 13 Nov night, which close the points D-305 left open. As recommended: only the Index team may open and read an Index question, so the people who train models see scores and question ids only (this narrows the rule that the foundation team sees every data set); at most 5 real calls among an edition's 20 incoming questions; the upkeep page is for ThinkLatent only; the Index agent watches saturation and the Index team hardens, with retiring a pillar left to the pillar council; the forecast shows to ThinkLatent only; a question keeps its side, edition or stage checks, never both; accuracy and made-up answers are shown as two numbers side by side, with no blended score (the 'hallucination-adjusted score' of the approved boards leaves by this decision); the Enterprise benchmark's questions count in their pillar and also give a score per category under Real Enterprise. Against the recommendation: outside models get a full run every month, with delta scoring in between, rather than a spot check each edition; and questions that leave an edition go back to the pool and may be brought in again in a later cycle, moving in and out at random so that no model can game the Index (this replaces the one-way life drawn in D-303). Both systems are to be drawn as catalogue pages: Call processing and Next best action. Changed on the boards: upkeep (a question's life, the pool by pillar as what the draw can choose from, who sees what), the edition's page, the queue, the offered set and Data sets. Not yet drawn: the two-number accuracy and made-up-answers columns, the benchmark programme page, the two system pages. The canvas has 67 boards.

Eight answers for what is left to draw, 13 Nov night. As recommended: the quarterly TL Index report is drafted by the Index agent, signed by the Head of ThinkLatent and open to everyone once signed; everyone sees a ThinkLatent model's size class and its cost per request, while the parameter count and machine cost show to ThinkLatent only; later-year features are carried on one 'What is coming' page in Help, by year, with a small 'Planned' line on the pages where they will live, and none is drawn in full now. The Playground: open to everyone at the Enterprise; sessions are private to the person, kept 30 days, never used for training and counted in usage without their text, and a session can be handed to a project as a starting prompt; no client data, with a notice and a check by the guardrail model on what is pasted. Nothing was drawn for these yet.

The Playground, 13 Nov night. Jithin wants it to be where anyone tries a TLM as they would try Claude.ai: advanced prompting, agentic behaviour, artifacts, files. Flagged by Claude and not resolved: a connector a person adds can bring client data in or carry text out without passing that check; LibreChat's client does not use the design kit, so the portal's kit-only rule needs a recorded exception; a restyled fork has to follow a fast-moving upstream. Scout brief written; nothing drawn yet for the Playground, and the simpler first draft was not published.

Shell theme opened, the first of the themes drawn before the build (D-284, D-312). The rest of Try TLM, four answers all as recommended, drawn the same hour on one board (Playground-Build); 77 boards, first draft with Jithin for review. Home, My work and the view across projects: four answers, all as recommended, drawn the same hour; 78 boards, first drafts with Jithin for review. Claude's note: 'every LibreChat feature on day one' (D-308) cannot hold as written until each collision is decided, and every feature kept is a set of screens to rebuild in the kit (D-311). Written up in scout-brief-librechat-features.md.

Which LibreChat features Try TLM keeps, eight answers after its code was read (D-321). Against the recommendation: memory is on, the person sees, edits and clears it and it is kept until cleared, so the 30 days of D-307 cover sessions only; everything LibreChat ships comes on day one, the experimental parts included; and image generation is on with one outside model ThinkLatent allows. Which outside model is not decided, and the Enterprise's Risk and IT security have not been asked; the board says it stays switched off in the build until they are. Taking everything on day one means about 35 areas of LibreChat's screens rebuilt in the kit (D-311) and kept in step with its releases; this is the largest single piece of the build and has no estimate yet.

The quality loop, four answers, drawn the same hour on one board (Project-QualityLoop, opened from the Quality tab); 80 boards, first draft with Jithin for review. Against the recommendation: the hand review of production is done by the project's two ThinkLatent people, not its members (the project sets the share reviewed); and every drift figure with its thresholds shows to the project's members, not only plain words. As recommended: the judge shows as Strong, Fair or Weak agreement with people, checked each month against fresh hand scores, a Weak judge is greyed and is not evidence until fixed, and the detail and bias checks sit behind the Engineering switch; findings are kept in a register on Quality with severity, owner, due date, state and what each holds back, and one closes only when its measure holds again for 7 days or an owner accepts it with a written reason on the record. Drawn: the review queue (lowest judge scores and longest calls first, then a daily sample, one in ten read again blind), one review with its three measures, the judge by measure, five drift measures with their figures and a weekly check of the project's own model against the foundation model, and the findings register. Claude's choices, not asked: an expected answer a reviewer writes is offered to the owners for the evaluation set and never becomes training data from there; 'Shifted' opens a finding; the gain over the foundation model opens a finding when the ranges meet for two weeks; the drift thresholds are sample values the project sets. Claude's note: two ThinkLatent people per project reviewing 2% of requests by hand is ThinkLatent's time, not the project's; at 26k requests a day on one feature that is about 500 reviews a day, where the board shows 240 a week, so the share or the staffing has to give. Not drawn and still half there: signal coverage by calling application, task and topic clusters with a privacy floor, numbered versions of a project's requirements, evaluators built from reviews, pairs of answers rated in the application.

Running a feature, four answers, drawn on one board (Feature-Flow, the feature's 'Models and flow' tab); 81 boards, first draft with Jithin for review. As recommended: the window switch of Home (today, 7 days, 30 days, quarter) is on every project and feature page, with one set of charts by day for requests, errors, availability and speed against what was agreed, with the worst day and the days over; a table 'Versions in service' on the feature page (live, on trial with its share, kept ready for 90 days, fallback), the word alias kept for engineers, and the trial share in the feature's header; requests by size show share, time, cost and quality one at a time on the same grid, with the busiest sizes listed with all four, engine timings staying behind the Engineering switch (D-291). Against the recommendation: sealed production text is asked for in the Enterprise's access management only; the portal takes no request and has no button for it (D-293 stands as written). Claude's choices, not asked: the by-day charts are drawn on the feature and said to sit on the project's Operations page too, but Project-Operations itself is not redrawn yet; quality in a cell with under 50 requests shows as a dash. Not drawn and still half there in this theme: temporary increases and limited requests by hour on shared endpoints, routing by task, hosting options, capacity by day, spend filters and showback by organization, tokens over the window, an agent's note on a trace.

The last four themes, eight answers, drawn on six boards the same hour; 87 boards, first drafts with Jithin for review. Jithin asked to finish them fast and get to the build. Against the recommendation: a training run's loss charts, over-fitting warning, GPU use per node and live log are all in the portal (the recommendation was to link the last two to the team's own tools). Claude's note: these six boards were drawn fast and each is thinner than the earlier ones; many half-there rows in these themes are still not on a board (training tiles and queue, graph ingestion, threshold history, hosting tiers, agent metrics at three levels, alerts detail, the weekly digest). With this the drawing of D-284 is declared ended by Jithin's ask to move to the build; the separate check of D-312 runs next and will say how much is still missing.
