decisions.by: Jithin (on a question with a recommendation)
decisions.decision: Registered as TL-022 fast-lane at Seed, its own row rather than a feature of TL-008, linked to TL-008, TL-004, TL-014 and TL-018; the scout brief (claude/scout-brief-fast-lane.md) is its doc. Scout finding recorded: 'over 1,000 tok/s' and '300 tokens in 200 ms' are different bars; the second needs about 1,700 to 2,000 tok/s per request once prefill and network are counted, and at 1,000 tok/s about 175 tokens fit in 200 ms

Run the three targets together: (a) over 1,000 tok/s per request on the Core 27B, (b) 300 tokens in 200 ms on the Core 27B, (c) the 200 ms class on the 7B Core where the TL Index shows it sufficient. Dissent recorded: the recommendation was (a) with 200 ms for replies of 150 tokens or fewer first, because (b) on H100 needs a drafter accepting about 6.9 tokens a step in FP8 (5.7 with 4-bit weights), beyond published chat results (DFlash on Gemma 4 31B: 3.0x on chat, 5.8x on math)

Prove the fast lane on one 8x H100 node from the ~16 H100s in hand, then scale out by adding H100 nodes as they come; the unit is one node (Core 27B as one TP8 replica, or the 7B Core as four TP2 replicas). Recorded with it: more H100s add capacity (about 0.5 to 0.8 million input tokens a minute per 27B unit and about 3 million or more per 7B unit, estimated), not per-request speed. Faster silicon (B300, Cerebras on AWS) is not decided: decisionsDue, recommended after the proof

Prompts average 1,000 to 10,000 tokens. Consequences recorded: 1 million input tokens a minute is 100 to 1,000 requests a minute; prefill becomes the largest cost inside 200 ms (about 146 ms for a 10,000-token prompt on the 27B on 8x H100), so 300 tokens in 200 ms is out of reach on the 27B on H100 at any prompt length and 150 tokens only up to about 3,250-token prompts without prefix-cache hits; the 7B Core at TP4 fits the whole range (156 to 182 ms for 300 tokens at drafter acceptance 4.0); one 27B unit carries about 0.7 to 0.8 million input tokens a minute at any prompt length (prefill-bound); the proof grid moves to 1,000, 4,000 and 10,000-token prompts with prefix-cache hit rates of 0%, 50% and 80%

One shared cluster for many applications: the gateway (Envoy with the ext_proc picker) diverts each call by bucket (prompt tokens x reply cap), service class, task and session, keeping an application's or session's calls on the same replica; each bucket publishes a per-range promise ('send requests in these ranges and you get these numbers'); pools are planned at each bucket's mean shape; idle replicas lend capacity to other buckets at lower priority. What is done now: dedicated, isolated machines per production use case

Every replica of a model runs the same vLLM settings, so buckets are routing groups and borrowing is instant; a bucket gets its own settings only where the proof shows a gain of 20% or more. Promises are p95 at the bucket's range edge plus a margin, and GPUs are sized at the bucket mean. Shared by default, with dedicated pools on request, per-application cache salt, priorities and quotas

Draft models (EAGLE-3, then DFlash) are trained by both routes, Speculators (vLLM-native) and Model Optimizer (NVIDIA's route), on the same target-written data, and compared on accepted length per bucket, tok/s per request and training hours. Dissent recorded: the recommendation was Speculators with Model Optimizer as a cross-check; both routes cost an extra training run per model

The proof is built as runnable code, not more answers: one Slurm job on one 8x H100 node runs public Gemma 4 31B (FP8, vLLM 0.33.0) through a drafter screen, the prompt x reply x in-flight grid, the small-model 200 ms class, layouts, mixed traffic behind the picker (capacity, policies, borrowing) and drafter training, then writes a report that judges pre-registered H1 to H10 and pushes results to GitHub. H7 to H10 added. Public drafters are tested first and our training is measured against them; the full plan keeps both training routes (D-377). The kit lives in thinklatent-labs/fast-lane, which Jithin creates

portfolio.horizonMixNote: Amended 2026-11-07 (D-133). Capacity is two people, so Now is capped at three rows and TL-007 runs without new build. This ranking is a judgement against the diagnosis, not the rubric: only TL-003 and TL-004 are scored. The next Portfolio session scores the Next rows. Role convention (2026-11-07): the lab is Jithin and the thinking partner; every named role (red-team seat, owner, lead, auditor, stream engineer) is assumed and played by one of the two until the lab moves into a company. Independence rule: a played critic or auditor runs in its own chat or a fresh agent that has not seen the build work, reading only the idea doc and register.
portfolio.diagnosis: The constraint on ThinkLatent is not model quality but evidence for adoption and governance throughput: owned models exist, and nothing proves to the business and Risk that they are sufficient and safe for a given workflow. Ideas that relieve this constraint come first.

spine.winningAspiration: Every model decision at the Enterprise runs on evidence, and most AI work runs on models the Enterprise owns, inside its own boundary, at lower cost and with clearer governance than renting frontier models by default.
spine.whereToPlay: Bounded, high-volume workflows (extraction, classification, routing, servicing, compliance pre-review) on Enterprise-built specialists; frontier models only where measured evidence shows a gain worth paying for. Not: general-purpose chat products, or competing with vendors on frontier capability.
spine.howToWin: Evidence nobody else has (the index on Enterprise tasks), an owned build-and-heal loop (TLM, compression, self-healing), and a governance path that approves usages faster than the side door.
spine.capabilitiesRequired: Evaluation register and harness; AI Gateway; HyperPod serving; compression pipeline; self-healing system; usage-approval record; contribution flow.
spine.managementSystems: The TL Index and its quarterly report, the Idea Register, the governance loop on the portal, and this lab.
